title_en: Peng Jiahui v. China Story Magazine — dispute over right to reputation
keywords_en: civil; dispute over right to reputation; first instance; intermediate people's court; Sichuan Province; Hubei Province; natural person; legal person; General Principles of the Civil Law; determination of reputation infringement; statute of limitations; protection of deceased person's reputation; novel fictionalizing and defaming a martyr; magazine publishing an apology; martyr's family filing a lawsuit; right to reputation; fraud; magazine's reputation dispute
full_text_en:
Peng Jiahui v. China Stories Magazine — dispute over the right to reputation

Plaintiff: Peng Jiahui, female, born on December 28, 1901, of Han ethnicity, residing in Chengdu City, Sichuan Province.

Agent ad litem: He Shifang and Lan Bo, lawyers of Xishu Law Firm, Chengdu City, Sichuan Province.

Defendant: China Stories Magazine. Domicile: Wuhan City, Hubei Province.

Responsible Person: Deng Deyuan, chief editor of the magazine.

Agent ad litem: Zheng Shi, lawyer of Desai Law Firm, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province;

Agent ad litem: Liang Yuanlin, deputy director of Hubei Provincial Mass Art Center.

The plaintiff, Peng Jiahui, filed a lawsuit with the Chengdu Intermediate People’s Court of Sichuan Province against the defendant, China Stories Magazine (hereinafter referred to as the Magazine), for a dispute over reputation infringement.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The story "The Calamity" written by Zhou Huang was published in Issue 4 of 1998 of China Stories magazine, which tampered with the history of her brother, martyr Peng Jiazhen, causing extremely adverse effects both domestically and internationally. Although the defendant expressed willingness to properly handle the matter, its published apology statement sought to evade responsibility, which is insufficient to restore the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen or to compensate for the mental and material losses suffered by his family members. She requested that the Magazine make a profound and solemn apology, eliminate the adverse effects at home and abroad, and pay RMB 465,000 for mental distress damages for infringement of martyr Peng Jiazhen’s reputation, and RMB 38,590 for material losses.

Defendant's Defense: The time when plaintiff Peng Jiahui filed the lawsuit had exceeded the statute of limitations; the Magazine had no obligation to verify the characters and events in popular fiction, nor was it possible to verify the circumstances of figures from the period of the Revolution of 1911. After learning that the novel "The Calamity" did infringe on the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen, the Magazine immediately made a public apology and took corrective measures, and thus did not constitute infringement against Peng Jiahui.

Facts Found by the Court of Chengdu Intermediate People's Court:

China Stories magazine is a bimonthly magazine primarily featuring fiction. Issue 4 of 1998 published the novel "The Calamity" written by Zhou Huang, which narrated a major fraud case that occurred in Shanghai in 1928, and devoted a large portion to the plot of Bai Liangyu, daughter of Qing Dynasty Military Councilor Liang Bi, seeking revenge for her father. The novel fictionalized the real event in which the historical figure of the Revolution of 1911, Peng Jiazhen, sacrificed his life while assassinating Military Councilor Liang Bi to overthrow the Qing Dynasty, by depicting Peng Jiazhen being caught on the spot during the assassination, escaping in the chaos, then serving the British intelligence agency, and finally being found and killed by Bai Liangyu. The novel portrayed Peng Jiazhen as a villain, describing him as a "demon." Dialogues in the novel included: "The revolutionaries sent Peng Jiazhen to assassinate your esteemed father; after all, it was not a personal grudge, and the people do not think he was wrong. But now this Peng Jiazhen is employed by the Black Widow, aiding the evil, so of course he deserves to be killed," "Peng Jiazhen, with your thin face, you cannot pretend to be a stout man; if you were an upright revolutionary, you would not become a mangy dog kept by the Black Widow…" The character Peng Jiazhen in the novel claimed: "I never change my name whether I sit or stand; I was once a resounding revolutionary, and now I am a personal bodyguard of the British Empire." The novel described Peng Jiazhen's death as follows: Peng Jiazhen "ignoring the excruciating pain of his severed hand, knelt on both knees and begged for mercy, saying: 'Miss, you have crippled my right hand, now please be merciful and spare my life,'" "Peng Jiazhen kowtowed repeatedly, saying: 'Miss, I have no grudge against you, I do not know you, please spare my life,'" etc. Additionally, the novel included fabricated content about Peng Jiazhen's improper relationships with women.

The Magazine's review of the novel "The Calamity" was clearly recorded in the "Manuscript Processing Form." The preliminary review opinion was: Behind a huge jewelry fraud case lay a very complex political struggle, both international and domestic. Therefore, the story was quite twisty, bizarre, and unexpected. The work truthfully reflected the social reality during the period of nationalist rule, with concise language and a plain writing style. The title could be changed or kept. The second review opinion was: Agree with the above evaluation and opinion; it can be accepted, but the wording needs polishing, with several coined terms; additionally, the title should be re-proposed, as it is not popular or通俗 enough. The final review opinion was: The fraud手法 seems familiar, but it is readable; agree with the above opinions.

On October 31, 2000, the Magazine received a fax from the Committee of the Grand General Peng Jiazhen Shrine (hereinafter referred to as "Peng Jiazhen Shrine") and four relatives of martyr Peng Jiazhen, including Peng Jiaxiang, regarding the infringement of martyr Peng Jiazhen's reputation by the novel "The Calamity." Upon learning of the situation, the Magazine immediately instructed the responsible editor to contact the author and replied to the Peng Jiazhen Shrine and Peng Jiaxiang et al., informing them that the issue was being addressed. On November 3, the Magazine sent personnel to Tianjin and Chengdu respectively to verify relevant facts with the author and the relatives of martyr Peng Jiazhen, and learned that the author Zhou Huang had passed away and that the novel "The Calamity" contained serious inaccuracies. Regarding the erroneous publication of the novel "The Calamity," the Magazine made the following decisions: 1. Suspend the relevant personnel from duty for investigation. 2. Issue a public statement of apology in relevant domestic media. 3. Publish a special article in China Stories about the heroic sacrifice of martyr Peng Jiazhen as soon as possible to set the record straight. On November 14 of the same year, the Magazine drafted a "Sincere Apology," the full text of which was: "In the work 'The Calamity' published in Issue 4, 1998 of China Stories, the author Zhou Huang made a serious distortion of historical facts regarding the death of Grand General Peng Jiazhen, a martyr of the Revolution of 1911 praised by Sun Yat-sen and Mao Zedong, who died heroically after assassinating Liang Bi on the night of January 26, 1912, causing significant harm to the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen and also hurting the feelings of his relatives. As the publisher of the article, China Stories deeply regrets the errors made during the review process and expresses our profound apology to martyr Peng Jiazhen and his relatives!" The Magazine published this "Sincere Apology" in the Wuhan Evening News, Chinese Culture Daily, China Cultural Relics News, Sichuan Daily, and Chengdu Evening News on November 16, November 19, and November 22, 2000, respectively. Issue 1, 2001 of China Stories also published a special article "Eternal Righteousness — A Record of Grand General Peng Jiazhen's Sacrifice for the Country" along with an editor's note. The full text of the editor's note was: "Peng Jiazhen, courtesy name Xiru. Born on April 9, 1888, in Yaodu Township, Jintang County, Sichuan (now Qingbaijiang District). In 1906, while inspecting military affairs in Japan, he joined the 'Tongmenghui.' After returning to China, he engaged in anti-Qing revolutionary activities in Chengdu, Kunming, Shenyang, Tianjin, Beijing, Shanghai, and other places. On January 26, 1912, he alone ventured into the tiger's den, threw a bomb to assassinate Liang Bi, the Military Councilor of the Qing government's Military Council and leader of the Imperial Clan Party, and died heroically for the country on the spot. We excerpt the following materials to highlight the martyr's glorious reputation." The special article included four pieces introducing martyr Peng Jiazhen, along with a "Revolutionary Martyr's Family Honorary Certificate" signed by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1953 and a photo of martyr Peng Jiazhen. After the special article, the full text of the "Sincere Apology" was reprinted in bold type, along with a statement: "Readers who hold Issue 4, 1998 of China Stories, please return it to our society for destruction; postage and magazine fees will be borne by the Magazine." On February 3, 2001, the Magazine sent a letter to the "Peng Jiazhen Shrine" and relatives of martyr Peng Jiazhen, including Peng Jiaxiang, informing them of the relevant handling situation and expressing hope for reaching an understanding and properly resolving the matter.

In late July 2001, Peng Jiahui filed a lawsuit with the People's Court. Because Peng Jiahui had not previously communicated with the Magazine, and the Magazine was unaware of Peng Jiahui's existence. When the Magazine learned that martyr Peng Jiazhen's sister Peng Jiahui was still alive, it sent a special person to visit Peng Jiahui, who was hospitalized, to express condolences and apologize.

The Chengdu Intermediate People's Court held:

Article 120, paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If a citizen's right to personal name, portrait, reputation, or honor is infringed upon, the citizen has the right to demand cessation of the infringement, restoration of reputation, elimination of adverse effects, and an apology, and may also demand compensation for losses." Article 140 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (Trial Implementation) provides: "Disclosing another person's privacy in written or oral form, fabricating facts to publicly defame another person's personality, or damaging another person's reputation through insults, slander, or other means, causing certain influence, shall be deemed as acts infringing upon a citizen's right to reputation." Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Determination of Liability for Compensation for Mental Damage in Civil Torts provides: "If a natural person dies due to an infringing act, or if the personality or remains of a natural person are infringed after death, and the spouse, parents, or children of the deceased file a lawsuit with the People's Court requesting compensation for mental damage, the spouse, parents, or children shall be listed as plaintiffs; if there is no spouse, parents, or children, other close relatives may file the lawsuit, and other close relatives shall be listed as plaintiffs." The novel "The Calamity" published in Issue 4, 1998 of China Stories, by fabricating plots and devoting a large portion to portraying martyr Peng Jiazhen, who heroically sacrificed himself in the Revolution of 1911, as a repulsive villain, seriously defamed the personality of martyr Peng Jiazhen and infringed upon his reputation. The facts are clear, the evidence is sufficient, and all parties have no objection to this. Since the parents of martyr Peng Jiazhen are deceased, and he had no spouse or children, the plaintiff Peng Jiahui, as the sister of martyr Peng Jiazhen, has the right to file a civil lawsuit against the unit or individual that infringed upon the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen.

Article 150 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (Trial Implementation) provides: "If a citizen's right to personal name, portrait, reputation, or honor, or a legal person's right to name, reputation, or honor is damaged, and the citizen or legal person demands compensation for losses, the People's Court may determine the amount of compensation based on the degree of fault of the infringer, the specific circumstances, consequences, and impact of the infringing act." The defendant, China Stories Magazine, bears the responsibility for failing to fulfill its review obligation regarding the infringement of martyr Peng Jiazhen's reputation by the novel "The Calamity." A publishing unit has the duty to review the works it publishes and should conduct a comprehensive review of the content of the works. In publishing literary works involving real events and persons, attention should be paid to verifying whether the relevant descriptions are true and whether they infringe upon the lawful rights of others. The content of the novel "The Calamity" is set against real historical events and persons; this is different from literary works whose content is entirely fictional. The character "Peng Jiazhen" in the novel is real, and the Magazine had the obligation to verify the truthfulness of the relevant descriptions and to ensure that the descriptions involving Peng Jiazhen in the novel did not infringe upon his lawful rights. As a well-known figure in the history of the Revolution of 1911, martyr Peng Jiazhen's experiences were not difficult to verify, but the Magazine failed to verify the truthfulness of the relevant descriptions, resulting in issues that could have been discovered during review not being discovered. The Magazine should bear corresponding responsibility for the publication of a work that seriously infringed upon the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen.

Article 135 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The statute of limitations for filing a lawsuit with the People's Court to protect civil rights is two years, unless otherwise provided by law." Article 137 provides: "The statute of limitations begins to run from the time when the right holder knows or should have known that his rights were infringed upon. However, if more than twenty years have passed since the infringement occurred, the People's Court will not provide protection. Under special circumstances, the People's Court may extend the statute of limitations." Although Issue 4, 1998 of China Stories was officially released in Chengdu City, Sichuan Province on July 1 of that year, the influence and distribution scope of the publication are limited. It cannot be assumed that after the publication is released, the public should know the content of the publication, thereby taking the publication and distribution date as the starting point for calculating the statute of limitations. Since the defendant Magazine cannot prove that Peng Jiahui knew the content of the novel "The Calamity" before July 1999, and the plaintiff adduced evidence that she only learned of the content of the novel "The Calamity" in April 2000 after other relatives received a reader's letter, given that Peng Jiahui was over 90 years old at the time and illiterate, her claim is more reasonable and should be accepted. After the negotiations between her relatives and the defendant Magazine failed, Peng Jiahui filed the lawsuit with the court in July 2001, which is within the statutory limitation period.

Article 8 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Determination of Liability for Compensation for Mental Damage in Civil Torts provides: "If mental damage is caused by an infringement, but no serious consequences have occurred, the victim's request for compensation for mental damage is generally not supported; the People's Court may, depending on the circumstances, determine that the infringer shall cease the infringement, restore reputation, eliminate adverse effects, and apologize. If mental damage is caused by the infringement and serious consequences occur, the People's Court may, in addition to ordering the infringer to bear civil liability such as ceasing the infringement, restoring reputation, eliminating adverse effects, and apologizing, also order the infringer to pay corresponding mental distress damages at the request of the victim." After learning that the novel "The Calamity" had infringed upon the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen, the defendant Magazine promptly explained the situation to Peng Jiazhen's relatives, published an apology in newspapers, published a special article commemorating martyr Peng Jiazhen in the most recent issue of China Stories, and took measures such as destroying copies of the magazine containing the infringing content, effectively stopping the infringement of martyr Peng Jiazhen's reputation, and in fact had already fulfilled its obligations of apology, restoration of reputation, and elimination of adverse effects. The plaintiff Peng Jiahui's request for compensation for mental losses has factual and legal basis and should be considered, but the plaintiff's request for compensation for hospitalization and other losses cannot be confirmed as caused by the Magazine's infringement and is not supported. Accordingly, the judgment is as follows:

1. The defendant, China Stories Magazine, shall compensate the plaintiff Peng Jiahui for mental losses in the amount of RMB 50,000, to be paid within ten days after this judgment takes legal effect;

2. The remaining claims of the plaintiff Peng Jiahui are dismissed.

The court acceptance fee for this case is RMB 1,550, to be borne by the defendant, China Stories Magazine.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, both the plaintiff and defendant disagreed and simultaneously appealed to the Sichuan High People's Court. The grounds of appeal of the Magazine were: 1. The statute of limitations for Peng Jiahui's lawsuit should be calculated from July 1, 1998, when Issue 4 of China Stories was distributed in Chengdu; Peng Jiahui's lawsuit filed two years later exceeded the statutory limitation period; 2. "The Calamity" is a work of fiction, not a news report or documentary work, and the publishing unit has no statutory obligation to verify the truth of the facts; 3. After learning that the novel "The Calamity" was infringing, the Magazine promptly took corrective measures, publishing a "Sincere Apology" statement in relevant media and later publishing a series of special articles commemorating martyr Peng Jiazhen in subsequent issues of China Stories, thereby fulfilling its obligations of apology, restoration of reputation, and elimination of adverse effects, and should not bear tort liability under the law; it requested the dismissal of Peng Jiahui's claims. Peng Jiahui's grounds of appeal were: 1. The Magazine shifted all causes and responsibilities for damaging the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen onto the deceased author, denying its own infringement, and its attitude was insincere; 2. The Magazine's remedial measures were not timely, and the adverse effects had not been eliminated; 3. The amount of compensation awarded by the Magazine was too low.

During the second-instance proceedings, the appellant Peng Jiahui died on April 9, 2002. The Sichuan High People's Court, pursuant to Article 136 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, ruled to suspend the proceedings. After five children of Peng Jiahui, namely Lin Qi, Lin Wei, Lin Zong, Gao Xuebing, and Lin Yuzhang, clearly expressed their intention to continue participating in the lawsuit, the proceedings were resumed.

The Sichuan High People's Court held that a citizen's right to reputation is protected by law, and any act of defaming another's reputation is prohibited by law; literary works are no exception. For literary works involving real events and persons, the publishing unit should verify whether the relevant content is true and whether it infringes upon the lawful rights of others. The Revolution of 1911 is of great significance in modern Chinese history, and evaluations of historical events and figures in the Revolution of 1911 should be serious and rigorous. Even the content of literary works should be consistent with the basic circumstances of historical events and figures; they must not distort historical facts, fabricate or fictionalize plots, or wantonly infringe upon the reputation of others. The novel "The Calamity" contains a large portion concerning events and figures of the Revolution of 1911. If the defendant Magazine had verified relevant historical materials during the review of the manuscript, it could easily have discovered the fabricated and fictionalized content in the work and determined whether it damaged the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen. However, the Magazine, during the preliminary, second, and final reviews of the manuscript, did not verify the authenticity of historical events and figures, demonstrating obvious subjective fault and should bear corresponding responsibility for the occurrence of the infringing result. Regarding the statute of limitations in this case, because the Magazine has no evidence to prove that Peng Jiahui knew of the infringement before July 1999 after the publication of Issue 4, 1998 of China Stories, it should be determined that the lawsuit filed by Peng Jiahui did not exceed the statutory limitation period. After learning of the infringement caused by the novel "The Calamity," the Magazine promptly took a series of remedial measures, fulfilling its obligations to cease the infringement, restore reputation, eliminate adverse effects, and apologize. Its attitude was sincere, and its actions were effective; it need not perform the above obligations again, but must pay corresponding mental compensation to the relatives of the deceased due to the infringement.

Peng Jiahui, as a close relative of martyr Peng Jiazhen, filed the lawsuit against the Magazine to uphold the reputation of martyr Peng Jiazhen, not because her own right to reputation had been infringed. The first-instance court's determination that the infringer's act of infringing upon the reputation of the deceased also constituted infringement against the close relatives of the deceased has no legal basis. Peng Jiahui's claim for compensation for losses incurred from hospitalization and treatment is not supported due to insufficient evidence proving they were caused by the Magazine's infringement; however, her claim for necessary travel expenses and photocopying expenses incurred from this lawsuit should be supported. After Peng Jiahui's death, the economic compensation she should receive shall be jointly inherited by her statutory heirs Lin Qi, Lin Wei, Lin Qiong, Gao Xuebing, and Lin Yuzhang. Accordingly, the judgment is as follows:

1. Affirm item 2 of the first-instance civil judgment of Chengdu Intermediate People's Court of Sichuan Province;

2. Amend item 1 of the first-instance civil judgment of Chengdu Intermediate People's Court of Sichuan Province to read: China Stories Magazine shall pay Peng Jiahui mental distress damages in the amount of RMB 50,000;

3. China Stories Magazine shall pay Peng Jiahui a total of RMB 500 for photocopying expenses and travel expenses incurred from this lawsuit;

4. China Stories Magazine shall pay the above amounts to Lin Qi, Lin Wei, Lin Qiong, Gao Xuebing, and Lin Yuzhang, to be completed within ten days after this judgment takes effect.

The acceptance fees for the first and second instances shall be borne by China Stories Magazine.
